slice: Money is in the hospitals and the AI labs. Diesel lingers. Someone still pays.

stories.title: Wall Street’s $10bn India hospital bet sparks a fight over bills
points: Blackstone, KKR, TPG, General Atlantic and others have put about $10 billion into Indian hospital chains in five years, per EY. PE-backed chains hold under 5% of beds but are strong in high-margin cardiac and cancer care.
In August a parliamentary panel warned of an “unchecked influx of foreign capital” and suggested revisiting foreign-investment rules, examining price caps and creating a hospital regulator.

Insurers say hospitals inflate bills and push costly procedures; hospitals blame late payments and low reimbursement. One Mumbai patient paid out of pocket when her insurer refused the robotic part of her surgery.
stories.why: Private money is building the beds India lacks, but patients and insurers are feeling the price.
stories.other: EQT’s Jean Eric Salata warns price regulation would deter investors, and Wharton’s Lawton Burns says it is unclear regulation can contain costs. Would caps mean fewer new hospitals?

stories.title: AI is junk food for the mind, an essay argues
points: The essay rejects the brain-as-computer model, drawing on neuroscientist Paul Cisek’s view of brains as feedback-control systems.
It calls AI a ‘cognitive hot dog’: harmless now and then, harmful as a regular diet, and most damaging in education.
It cites a study from China in which thousands of students largely stopped doing homework once they started using AI, hurting their learning.
stories.why: Learning takes effort; a tool that removes the effort can remove the learning.
stories.other: Calculators and writing raised similar fears, though the author argues AI is different in kind. Used as a tutor rather than a shortcut, could it deepen learning?

stories.title: Indian banks move from buying AI to owning a piece of it
points: HDFC Bank’s stake in CoRover, maker of BharatGPT, is described as the first by a leading private bank in a model maker; Canara Bank’s VC arm had already invested.
IDFC FIRST Bank and Sarvam are building an R&D lab for a “self-improving bank”, with systems that learn from customer interactions, human corrections and outcomes.
Bajaj Finance took 5% of video-avatar startup TrueFan AI, under a programme to invest ₹1,500–2,000 crore in early-stage AI, cybersecurity and fintech startups.
stories.why: A stake gives banks a say in the AI roadmap they increasingly depend on.
stories.other: The article itself calls it an open question whether this spreads beyond the biggest, most AI-forward lenders. For a startup, a client that is also investor and co-developer has a lot of leverage. Partnership, or dependence?

stories.title: Indian Railways is 99.6% electrified, but diesel isn’t going away
points: About 69,873 of 70,142 broad-gauge route km were electrified by March 2026, up from 18,927 km in 2009-10.
Traction diesel fell from 293 crore litres in 2015-16 to 108 crore litres in 2024-25, about 63%; the ministry puts electrification savings at around ₹6,000 crore.
Diesel stays for grid failures, shunting, hill and narrow-gauge lines and new Northeast routes; 100 new diesel locos were commissioned in each of 2022-23 and 2023-24.
stories.why: Every litre of diesel not burned cuts India’s exposure to imported crude.
stories.other: Amit Shah says railway diesel use will reach zero by 2030, yet 200 new diesel locos joined in two years and the new LNG train still runs partly on diesel. Sensible backup, or a long tail?

stories.title: A prediction market for the past: bet on ‘disputed facts’
points: Verifact Markets, launched on Friday, lets traders bet “true” or “false” on disputed past events, from Covid-19’s origins to whether Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide.

It is backed by Positron Capital Management, tech investor Peter Wokwicz’s family office; it runs on-chain with stablecoins and, as it is not a licensed US exchange, is open only outside the US for now.
Prices alone won’t decide truth, says CEO Rodrigo Aquino: users submit evidence, and if the company can’t make a call it ‘expires’ the market and pays out on its odds.
stories.why: It treats contested facts as something a market can price.
stories.other: Its method for deciding truth is vague and, in Aquino’s word, ‘very secretive’, and crowds can be confidently wrong. Yet paying for credible evidence might surface documents others miss. Truth engine, or betting on conspiracies?

stories.title: Javed Anwer’s satire: lose your job so AI can remake the world
points: Sam Altman said on a Politico podcast that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of AI.
Anwer answers with mock praise, ranking job losses, AI-run weapons and synthetic viruses as small prices to pay for a promised utopia.
His real target is the gap between tech leaders’ grand vision and everyone else’s 9-to-5 jobs, EMIs and dinner tables.
stories.why: It asks who carries AI’s costs while its builders collect the gains.
stories.other: Read charitably, Altman is being frank that every big technology brings harm alongside benefit. Is mockery fair to a call for realism about trade-offs?
